title: How to un-Big Tech your online life
author: David Pierce

recommendations.name: Mario Tennis Fever
recommendations.blurb: The N64 version of Mario Tennis is probably my favorite video game of all time — Luigi, left-handed, I was unbeatable — and no tennis game has ever quite lived up to it.

recommendations.name: Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die
recommendations.blurb: I wasn’t sure about the trailer for this one, but by all accounts this is a wacky, weird, perfectly timed movie about time travel and saving humanity. The premise reminds me a little of Safety Not Guaranteed, an extremely underrated movie.

recommendations.name: Wes Cook and The McDonald’s Mural
recommendations.blurb: “ Wes Cook and The McDonald’s Mural.” Remember that amazing Cabel Sasser XOXO talk from a couple of years ago? Well, Sasser has finally written out the whole story of saving the mural, and shared some truly incredible photos of the process.

recommendations.name: The Sony WF-1000XM6
recommendations.blurb: The “best earbuds” competition pretty much comes down to Sony vs. Apple, and while I much prefer the look of these to any AirPod, it’s a bummer to hear it can be hard to find the right fit with them. If I can get these to stay in my ear, I may be $330 poorer here in a few days.

recommendations.name: The Interface
recommendations.blurb: Fun, informative, thoughtful new podcast from the BBC, hosted by three tech journalists I admire. I don’t know if it’ll always be this mix of news and history, or if Karen Hao will keep being so hilariously mean to her cohosts, but I dig it all so far.

recommendations.name: Fitbit’s personal health coach
recommendations.blurb: Like my colleague Vee Song, I kind of hate AI coaches. But also like Vee, I think Fitbit is up to something interesting here — rather than an annoying cheerleader, Fitbit is trying to build a more interactive, more understandable set of wellness tools, and that I can get behind.

recommendations.name: Seedance 2.0
recommendations.blurb: It is my general belief that generative AI tools are a bad thing. But if you like these creative tools, this new model from ByteDance — which you can prompt with a combination of text, images, audio, and video — appears to be kind of blowing people’s minds.

recommendations.name: YouTube for Vision Pro
recommendations.blurb: Are there any Vision Pro users out there? Maybe? I don’t know. But if you do still use your headset, a native YouTube app is actually a big deal. I’m curious to see if this helps get more people making immersive content again.

recommendations.name: Proton
recommendations.blurb: Almost everybody who told me they’re ditching Google told me they’re moving to Proton. And with good reason! Proton does email, calendar, docs, file storage, and more, and does it all really well. This is the first place I’d tell almost anyone to start.

recommendations.name: Signal
recommendations.blurb: The messaging app of choice, by a mile. Like Proton, it is an incredibly privacy-focused tool that is still easy and nice to use. I have nothing but good feelings about Signal.

recommendations.name: Nextcloud
recommendations.blurb: This one I did not expect! It’s another suite of services, with a lot of impressive features, but in addition to everything else it is open-source and can even be self-hosted.

recommendations.name: Home Assistant
recommendations.blurb: For the smart home crowd, there is really only one choice.

recommendations.name: Kagi
recommendations.blurb: Lots of folks are replacing Google Search with either Kagi or Ecosia. As for browsers, it was pretty much all Firefox.

recommendations.name: Linux Mint
recommendations.blurb: Linux Mint came up a bunch as a user-friendly way out of the Big Tech operating systems. It’s harder to get away from Android and iOS, but GrapheneOS is a popular alternative for mobile.

recommendations.name: Jellyfin
recommendations.blurb: Jellyfin appears to be the media platform of choice. Some Plex love, too, but mostly Jellyfin.

recommendations.name: Obsidian
recommendations.blurb: Obsidian, one of my favorite note-taking apps, is a favorite as well. Since it’s built on text files, it is futureproof, unlike virtually any other software you’ll find.

recommendations.name: Garmin smartwatches
recommendations.blurb: Oh boy do you all love Garmin smartwatches! I’m still a little skeptical that they work for anyone other than hardcore fitness folks, but you all love them as Apple and Pixel Watch alternatives.

recommendations.name: Sunbeam F1
recommendations.blurb: The Sunbeam F1 flip phones, which actually look like they offer a pretty clever set of features, have some very devoted smartphone-ditching fans out there.

recommendations.name: Playdate
recommendations.blurb: Couple of votes for the Playdate, too, as a less intense way to game.

recommendations.name: Boox
recommendations.blurb: I got lots of E Ink device recommendations. Boox gear came up a lot. The Xteink X4, the little e-reader that sticks to the back of your phone, seems to have captured some hearts out there.

recommendations.name: Just a regular iPhone 15, though I keep eyeing a refurbished 13 mini
recommendations.blurb: The phone: Just a regular iPhone 15, though I keep eyeing a refurbished 13 mini. Bring back small phones!

recommendations.name: Bluesky
recommendations.blurb: On top of some standard Apple apps, Signal, and Bluesky, I have Norwegian web browser Vivaldi, Bulgarian feed reader Inoreader, French streaming service Deezer, and Proton Mail from Switzerland.

recommendations.name: Anbernic RG34XXSP
recommendations.blurb: Loving my new Anbernic RG34XXSP! It’s perfect for playing GBA games because of the clamshell design and 3:2 aspect ratio screen. MinUI (OS) also makes it a very focused experience. Currently playing through The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap for the first time.

recommendations.name: I Photoshop Paddington into a movie, TV show, or pop culture until I forget
recommendations.blurb: Currently very into these two Bluesky accounts. They both bring me so much joy: I Photoshop Paddington into a movie, TV show, or pop culture until I forget, and Inserting a Muppet into a Star Trek screenshot.

recommendations.name: Maxell Japanese cassette player
recommendations.blurb: I’ve been using my Maxell Japanese cassette player more and more. I found a shop in Roma Norte where it feels like a super cool hunting trip, digging for music I like on cassette.

recommendations.name: Jujutsu Kaisen
recommendations.blurb: Watching the new season of Jujutsu Kaisen and it’s a masterpiece so far! Every episode is an art piece. Same thing with Frieren.

recommendations.name: Frieren
recommendations.blurb: Watching the new season of Jujutsu Kaisen and it’s a masterpiece so far! Every episode is an art piece. Same thing with Frieren.

recommendations.name: Stardew Valley
recommendations.blurb: I’m in Michigan and this winter has been long and cold. Stardew Valley had been a remedy until I got to winter there as well. The relief I felt when it became spring last night was palpable. Now waiting for the real thing.

recommendations.name: Wispr Flow
recommendations.blurb: I’ve been totally into AI dictation tools like Wispr Flow, Willow, and Raycast. I’m so much faster speaking than typing. They work seamlessly on Mac but have some friction on iOS due to permissions. Makes me think this will be baked into future versions of Mac/iOS natively.

recommendations.name: NewsMap
recommendations.blurb: NewsMap has been helping me get a bird’s eye view of current events. It’s a ‘squarified tree map visualization of Google News.’ Runs as a web app and is customizable. Quick, easy color coded news in a handy grid format.

recommendations.name: Gizmo
recommendations.blurb: I was sitting waiting to see The 25th Annual Putnam Spelling Bee in NYC, and a few rows in front of me a girl was scrolling what looked like a TikTok feed, but was filled with little mini-app toys that seemed impossibly varied and unending. A quick Google turned it up: a new app called Gizmo.

recommendations.name: how a stadium handles two huge events in a row
recommendations.blurb: So in the span of a few days, we were treated to an inside look at how a stadium handles two huge events in a row, a deep look at the NFL’s obsession with growing its international audience, an hourlong podcast about the pregame flyover, a great vlog about life as a sports photographer, and so much…
